data.title: Middle East Eye: Houthis won't seize Aden, Yemeni government forces say
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Houthis won't seize Aden, Yemeni government forces say
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have pushed as close as 60km to Aden, the temporary capital of the country's internationally recognised government, but they will not capture the city, Yemen's military said on Tuesday.
"I'll speak to you frankly. The situation is not where we want it to be. But it's not as dire as reported," Colonel Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaily, spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces, told a group of reporters via video link.
Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from the internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers.
Aden, now the target of Houthi missile and drone strikes, had previously not seen major hostilities since street battles in 2015, soon after the internationally recognised government fled Houthi-run Sanaa and made the port city its base.
Reporting by Reuters

data.title: Middle East Eye: US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
A US federal judge on Monday permanently barred the Trump administration from punishing rights groups who liaise with the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ruling extends to all Americans, and not just the plaintiffs in the case.
Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York first issued a temporary injunction last month.
This week he ruled that while "the Government effectively requests that the Court reconsider its earlier decisions ... there is no merit to that request".
"Put simply, Plaintiffs demonstrate that the Services Prohibition is a content-based restriction on speech and that it is not narrowly tailored to serve compelling state interests," Furman wrote.

Germany's left-wing Die Linke party expels pro-Palestine lawmaker
Germany's far-left Die Linke party on Tuesday expelled local pro-Palestine lawmaker Vanessa Emde over her criticism of Israel.
Die Linke, which came first in local elections in Berlin in September, has been trying to hammer out a coalition deal with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens.
Emde was newly elected as a local representative from the Neukolln district, which has a large Arab population.
Emde's expulsion on Tuesday - which was backed by more than two-thirds of Die Linke's lawmakers in the Berlin parliament - clears one potential hurdle to sealing a coalition deal with the SPD and the Greens.

“Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, [and] be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status,” Kushner said in an interview with New York Magazine.
The remarks are notable given Kushner’s longtime advocacy for Israel and efforts to put it at the centre of a new regional security architecture in the Middle East.
Kushner is a longtime family friend of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and created the controversial Board of Peace which was supposed to oversee Gaza’s reconstruction.

Netanyahu called the UN a “swamp of antisemitism” that had to be drained.

Their candidate is Lana Nusseibeh, a British-educated diplomat from an old Palestinian family, who served as the UAE’s permanent representative to the UN from 2013 to 2024.
During those years, the country she represented actively worked against everything the UN was trying to do to stabilise the Middle East and Africa.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Unlawful de facto exemption': US sitting on 12-year backlog of alleged Israeli rights violations
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
'Unlawful de facto exemption': US sitting on 12-year backlog of alleged Israeli rights violations
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 18:17
A report from the Office of The Inspector General has raised concerns that the US has given Israel an 'exemption' from the Leahy Law
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pictured last month (Oliver Contreras/AFP)
Off
The US Department of State has a 12-year backlog of alleged cases of gross human rights violations in Israel to adjudicate, because the agency has made little effort to trace the end point of US military assistance there, a report quietly posted online by the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) last month showed.
The findings "demonstrate that the Department has created an unlawful de facto exemption to the law for Israel", Charles Blaha, a state department official who retired in 2023, wrote in a piece for Just Security on Monday.
The OIG report hones in on the application of the Leahy Law, which prohibits US assistance to any foreign security forces unit if the secretary of state has credible information that such a unit has committed "gross violations of human rights".
In a September 2025 report to Congress, the state department said the only units it had assessed to be ineligible for US security assistance were in Ukraine, Egypt and Jordan - even though Israel had previously been cited as having non-traceable assistance (NTA).
The NTA means the state department "cannot identify recipient units in advance of the transfer of assistance or training, or the units are not known with sufficient detail to make Leahy vetting possible", the OIG report said.
It concluded that the state department "had not developed or distributed comprehensive guidance and training to help staff implement NTA vetting requirements", and that nearly half of all missions overseas "did not respond to annual requirements to certify if a country was receiving NTA".

data.title: Middle East Eye: Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has said Baghdad will take over all of Kurdistan's border crossings and several oil fields that the autonomous region controls, in a move that was widely condemned by the region’s leaders as a step to clip their autonomy.
Baghdad’s decision comes at a time of internal division in the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and as the Middle East braces for a potential new US-Israeli attack on Iran.
Under American pressure, Zaidi recently attempted to crack down on Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Shia militia in Iraq aligned with Iran, which officials in Baghdad say has earned hundreds of millions of dollars from smuggling oil.
Zaidi's spokesperson Sabah al-Numan said on Tuesday that, based on those findings, Baghad would take control of "all border crossings in the Kurdistan Region".
